title: Bigs Who Pass or Shoot Threes
brief: Which big men add assists or threes on top of rebounds and blocks, giving rare category combinations? It must explain why combining categories that do not usually go together carries extra value in H2H.
summary: Big men who add assists or threes to their rebounds and blocks are worth extra in our 9-cat H2H league, because one roster slot fills categories that usually need two players. Threes from a big usually cost some FG% and some rebounds, so pay full price only when the FG% holds. Otherwise, use stretch bigs in punt FG% builds. Most passing bigs also give up turnovers, so they fit punt TO builds.

paragraphs.text: One expert rule is simple. A player who combines categories that do not normally go together, like rebounds and assists, carries extra value. A typical big gives rebounds, blocks and often FG%. Assists and threes usually come from other players. A big who adds one of them covers two groups of categories from one roster slot.

This matters in our format. Each week you win or lose each of the 9 categories against one opponent. We start 10 players and draft only 12 each. When one big already gives you assists or threes, your guard and wing slots and your remaining budget can go to the categories you still lack. One note calls a big with blocks, threes, rebounds and good FG% a fantasy cheat code.

sections.heading: The cost: threes pull against FG%

paragraphs.text: Threes and FG% pull against each other, so adding threes to a big man build is hard. FG% is a team ratio in our league. A big who takes many shots moves it a lot. A stretch big who shoots threes on volume can drag your team FG% down.

A center who takes more threes plays farther from the rim. His offensive rebounds and rim finishing tend to drop, while his assists and three-point attempts go up. So a big who moves outside often trades some rebounds and FG% for threes and assists. He does not simply add threes to an unchanged stat line.

The notes pull in different directions here. One side says the full package of blocks, threes, rebounds and good FG% is a cheat code. The other side says threes and FG% work against each other, and more threes means fewer offensive rebounds and fewer rim finishes. Read together, they say the full package exists but is rare. Pay a premium only when the FG% is still good. Treat a big with threes and a weak FG% as a punt FG% piece, not a cheat code.

sections.heading: How to use this in our auction

paragraphs.text: Pick your build before 2026-10-18. Most passing bigs in our pool give back turnovers, and their profiles point to punt TO builds. If you plan to punt TO, the assist bigs are the main targets for you. Their turnovers cost you nothing there, and their frontcourt assists count in full.

Many stretch bigs in our pool have FG% as their weak spot. Their profiles point to punt FG% builds. If you plan to punt FG%, these bigs give you threes, rebounds and blocks while their missed shots cost you nothing. If you plan to win FG%, look for stretch bigs whose FG% is not flagged as weak.

Pay for the combination, not for a tag. Before you bid, check that the player gives a real edge in both groups: rebounds or blocks, plus assists or threes. Several stretch bigs sit at the end of our 144-player pool. They are fine last picks, but they should not pull money away from your core.

sections.heading: What to check after the draft

paragraphs.text: In the first weeks, watch any big whose three-point attempts rise. Check at the same time whether his rebounds and FG% fall. If his assists and threes go up while his FG% drops, move him toward a punt FG% plan, or trade him to a manager who punts FG%. Do this before the trade deadline on 2027-03-04.

Waivers run daily on FAB, with at most 6 adds per week. Bench bigs who shoot threes sit on waivers and can matter fast when a starter ahead of them misses time. Keep a short watch list. Spend FAB when the minutes open up, not before.
